name: The Busanjin Crape Myrtles (Yangjeong-dong)

location.address: Jeongmyosa shrine grounds, Hwaji Park, San 73-28, Yangjeong 1-dong, Busanjin-gu, Busan, South Korea

access: Free entry to Hwaji Park and the Jeongmyosa shrine grounds. The site is also an active ancestral shrine (tomb of Jeong Mun-do, founder of the Dongnae Jeong clan) and family-owned/managed, so access is open but visitors are asked to be respectful.
transport: Busan Metro Line 1, Yangjeong Station, about 1.5 km / roughly 20 minutes on foot
verify_notes: TWO named trees (east and west) designated as ONE Natural Monument, No. 168, on 1965-04-07 (South Korea's Cultural Heritage Administration / heritage.go.kr, official government register, quantity listed as 2). Korean Wikipedia (fetched directly) and a 2026-07 travel feature (thetravelnews.co.kr, fetched directly) corroborate: planted, per Dongnae Jeong clan tradition, one on each side of the Goryeo-period tomb of clan founder Jeong Mun-do, making the traditional age roughly 800 years as of the 1965 designation (so closer to 860 today) -- this is a TRADITIONAL/genealogical dating, not a growth-rate estimate, kept broad and repeated as vaguely as the sources give it. The original trunk of at least one tree reportedly rotted away long ago, with surviving peripheral growth continuing as what now reads as multiple stems/trees from one historic planting -- this is documented regrowth, not evidence of death; the 2026 travel article confirms both trees are alive and blooming (peak late July to mid-August, red flowers). Largest trunk height given as 8.3 m; no girth recorded in any source found. Owner/manager of record is the Dongnae Jeong Clan Association. Location precision is APPROXIMATE: the register gives a plot number (San 73-28) within Hwaji Park rather than tree-level coordinates, and the Wikidata coordinate used here has not been independently confirmed against a photo or aerial image. Compact ensemble (two trunks at one shrine site, one obvious place to stand), fits the compact-famous-ensemble rule. name: The Suyeong Fortress Gomsol (Black Pine)
species: Black Pine / Japanese Black Pine (Pinus thunbergii)

location.address: Suyeong Historic Park (Suyeongseong Site), 43 Suyeongseong-ro, Suyeong-dong, Suyeong-gu, Busan, South Korea

access: Free, public historic park (Suyeong Historic Park / Suyeongseong Site), open to visitors as an ordinary city park and historical education site.
transport: Busan Metro Lines 2 and 3, Suyeong Station Exit 1, about 9 minutes on foot
verify_notes: Official Natural Monument No. 270, designated 1982-11-09 (or -04 per one Korean Wikipedia summary; the heritage.go.kr register itself gives 1982-11-09 -- flagging the one-day discrepancy rather than picking a winner). South Korea's Cultural Heritage Administration register (heritage.go.kr, fetched directly) confirms designation, species (Gomsol / Pinus thunbergii, a coastal black pine locally called haesong) and address; Korean Wikipedia (fetched directly) adds measurements: height 23.6 m, circumference (girth) 4.50 m -> girth_cm 450, trunk clear to first branch 7.0 m, estimated age roughly 400 years (attributed to local guidance/interpretive material rather than a growth-rate calculation, so kept as a broad band). A 2026 citizen-reporter piece (v.daum.net) independently describes the tree as well-maintained and alive today, standing in Suyeong Historic Park alongside a 17th-century fortress gate and Imjin War memorials; local legend holds that Joseon-era naval garrison soldiers regarded the pine as sacred and prayed to it for safety. The park also holds a second Natural Monument tree (Q-code not checked, a pujo-namu/Aphananthe aspera, No. 311) and several protected but undesignated gomsol nearby 250-300 years old -- out of scope for this brief but worth a future pass reaching toward the 4-tree floor for Busan.
